k-1.x_notes: Strengths: six substantial problems on actual-size gridded boards, all checked correct. P1 mixes coverable shapes (hexagon, 2x2 rhombus, chevron) with uncoverable ones: one odd, plus two even-area shapes (side-2 triangle, 8-triangle trapezoid) that fail because of the up/down imbalance, so it is a real entry to kernel 1. P2 asks for the fewest greens on side-2/3/4 triangles (2, 3, 4). P3 asks for all tilings and gives exactly the right number of copies (2 + 3). P4 asks for the fewest blocks (3, 3, 4); the side-3 triangle has a non-obvious 3-trapezoid answer that beats hexagon plus 3 greens. P5 is a placement game whose answers check out (1, 2, 1, 1, 2). P6 asks for all 6 tilings of a 16-triangle hexagon. Concrete, short wording, rules stated once. Weaknesses: parts are ambitious for kindergartners (judging who can always win, finding all 6 tilings), so they lean on the adult. The number of copies quietly tells children how many tilings exist. The footer has no id.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: actual-size outline puzzles with no internal grid (sailboat, cat, arrow, star, long hexagon, mountain), which is a classic accessible pattern-block entry. The chevron star and arrow are real fitting puzzles. The header and footer, including the id, match the format. Weaknesses: every task is 'fill this shape' with no impossibility, no counting of all ways, and no optimization, so the kernel is essentially absent. That is exactly the 'too dumbed down' complaint. Only five quick problems, so it is likely to run out well before 40 minutes. Cutesy picture names and extra headings ('Sailboat', 'Cat', 'First filling/Another filling'). 'Fill it again with any pieces' adds repetition without new thinking. 'Ask an adult to trace' adds procedure.
k-1.reason: X gives K-1 real mathematics (impossible boards, fewest gaps, all tilings, a strategy game) on usable gridded boards with plenty of work. Y is a short set of fill-the-picture puzzles that hits the organizer's explicit complaint about K-1 pages being dumbed down and ending early.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: a rich, well-sequenced, correct development of kernel 1. P1 has two coverable boards, one odd board, and one even-area trapezoid that fails by imbalance. P2 adds holes: E fails by colour, G is balanced and coverable (verified), and the bowtie F is balanced but impossible, which shows that balance is not enough. P3 asks for the fewest greens on triangles of side 2-5 with a proof for side 5. P4 generalizes to side 10 and side 100. P5 compares chevrons in a table and asks openly whether they can ever do better. P6 asks children to invent a 20-triangle board needing 6 greens (feasible). P7 asks for the rule for two greens on the side-2 hexagon (verified: it works exactly when one points up and one down) and gives small hexagons for recording. Boards are actual size, there is enough writing space, and the wording is concise. Weaknesses: seven problems is more than 40 minutes, though that is good stretch. The footer has no id. P6 and P7 are demanding for second graders.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: correct and on-kernel. P2 (fewest gaps on triangles of side 2-5, then 'explain why you cannot leave fewer') is the core idea. In P3, six boards with blues versus chevrons (checked: 0/0, 0/4, 0/0, 0/2, 1/1, 2/4) show that chevrons are never better. Actual size, clear recording blanks, and the footer has an id. Weaknesses: both impossible boards in P1 fail only by odd area, so the even-area colouring obstruction appears only implicitly in P2. The closing hint 'Can you cover one purple exactly with blues?' gives away the key idea. P2's title and instructions are repeated on a second page. There is little room to write explanations (one line in P3). Only three problems, with no generalization, design task, or holes.
grades-2-3.reason: Both are correct and on-kernel, but X develops the coloring obstruction much further (holes, a balanced-but-disconnected board, generalization, invention, the two-green rule) without giving away the key idea. Y is thinner and hints at its punchline.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: a strong arc through kernel 2, with every printed covering verified. P1 asks for all 6 tilings of the (1,2,2) hexagon and why the list is complete, with 10 recording boards so the count is not given away. P2 builds the flip graph and asks for the farthest pair (4). P3 has concrete flip tasks on the actual-size side-2 hexagon; the given pairs decode to 3, 4, and 8 flips. P4 asks for a 4-flip round trip from A (one exists) and whether 5 or 7 flips are possible (no, the graph is bipartite). P5 introduces ribbons with a correct worked example on a different board. P6 asks for a parity proof and a proven lower bound of 8 for E to F. P7 asks to count the 20 tilings, and P8 asks to count the (1,3,3) board (20). Concrete work comes before abstraction, and the open prompts leave the discoveries to the children. Weaknesses: the P5 ribbon definition is a dense paragraph and mixes the Problem 1 board with the hexagon board. The later proof and counting problems are hard for 4th graders and may need the mathematician's help. The small reference pictures in P3 are small. The footer has no id.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: correct throughout. The six cards are exactly the 6 tilings, and the flip map (shortest route A to F is 4, no odd returns) and the ribbon examples all check out. Accessible and orderly, with a useful line-joining-centres recording method, actual-size board, and footer id. Weaknesses: everything stays on the 6-tiling (1,2,2) board, so there is no bigger hexagon, no proof task, and no counting beyond C(4,2). The investigation is broken into ten tiny directed steps. Printing all six tilings on cards in P2 gives away P1. P7 ('write every order of LLRR, match to cards') and P10 ('circle every neighboring RL or LR... can you flip there?') print the intended discovery. There are routine 'check with your blocks' and 'write three examples' instructions. Strong 5th graders will run out of depth.
grades-4-5.reason: X keeps the method open and carries the ideas from the small board to the 20-tiling hexagon, parity proofs, and counting, all with correct examples. Y is correct and accessible but spoon-fed: it hands over the tilings and the flip and ribbon discovery in small steps.

overall.reason: X is better in every band. It is mathematically richer and fully correct, concrete on actual-size gridded boards, and leaves the thinking to the children; its fixes (footer ids, trimming) fit easily in fifteen minutes. Y is correct but thin: its K-1 pages are the dumbed-down, early-ending packet the organizer has complained about, and its 4-5 pages give away the discoveries, which fifteen minutes of editing cannot fix.
